question: Did Saxe-Weimar and Saxe-Eisenach become ONE territorial polity in law after 1741?
evidence_text_summary: The 1741 reunion of Saxe-Weimar and Saxe-Marcksuhl properties formed the duchy of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.
interpretation: A heading created for cataloguing convenience. It tells us the composite NAME was in use from 1741; it makes no statement about sovereignty or administration.
notes: Explicitly not treated as constitutional authority.

question: Did Saxe-Weimar and Saxe-Eisenach become ONE territorial polity in law after 1741?
exact_locator: Archivportal Thueringen, Bestand 26508 'Landesregierung Eisenach' (Landesarchiv Thueringen - Hauptstaatsarchiv Weimar)
evidence_text_summary: The superior authorities in Eisenach - Regierung, Kammer and Oberkonsistorium - administered the Eisenach Landesteil and were dissolved only by the administrative reform of 1849/50, when all superior authorities were concentrated in Weimar and the Eisenach archive was transferred to Weimar in 1850 and 1866.
interpretation: Eisenach still had its OWN central government, treasury and consistory in 1756. Two separate administrations under one ruler is the definition of a personal union, not of a merged state.
notes: Collection-level reading: the Vorwort page could not be rendered directly, so confidence is MEDIUM rather than HIGH.

question: Who ruled at 1756-08-01 and under which style?
exact_locator: Deutsche Biographie sfz39202, 'Ernst August II.' (Ernst August Constantin), 1737-1758
evidence_text_summary: Ernst August II Constantin (1737-1758) is styled Herzog von Sachsen-Weimar-Eisenach; he succeeded in 1748 as a minor, took self-government in 1755 and died in 1758, so he was the ruling duke at the snapshot date. A separate administrator acted in Eisenach during the minority.
interpretation: One person, both duchies. A separate administrator for Eisenach during the minority points the same way as the archival evidence: one ruler, two administrations.
notes: The composite STYLE is exactly what must not be mistaken for a merged territory.

question: Does the contemporary cartography treat Weimar and Eisenach as one drawn territory?
exact_locator: Sheet title, view f1: 'SECTIO INFERIOR, DVCATVM VINARIENSEM nec non ISENACENSIS Partes Boreales et Orientales'
evidence_text_summary: The 1747 sheet names the Duchy of Weimar AND, separately, the northern and eastern PARTS of Eisenach, and carries a lettered list of Weimar Aemter distinct from them.
interpretation: A contemporary cartographer working for the Saxon court still enumerated them separately six years after 1741.
notes: Read from the raster, not from a catalogue description.
